title: Data Structures & Algorithmic Complexity
description: Validates computational Big-O complexity, amortized array growth, balanced trees, shortest path graphs, and dynamic programming.

questions.question: Why does a dynamically resizing array (e.g. std::vector or ArrayList) achieve amortized O(1) insertion time when doubling capacity?
options: Because copying elements to a new array takes O(1) hardware time.
The costly O(N) reallocation occurs exponentially less frequently, spreading the reallocation overhead evenly across N insertions.
The array allocates virtual memory pages without executing memory copies.
Compilers optimize dynamic arrays into linked lists behind the scenes.
questions.explanation: Doubling size means copying takes 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + N = 2N operations across N insertions. Total operations / N = constant, yielding an amortized time of O(1) per append.

questions.question: What is the primary architectural trade-off between an AVL Tree and a Red-Black Tree?
options: AVL trees support duplicate keys; Red-Black trees strictly disallow them.
AVL trees are more rigidly balanced (height diff <= 1), yielding faster O(log N) lookups but requiring more rotations during frequent insertions and deletions than Red-Black trees.
Red-Black trees require O(N) space per node for color bits.
AVL trees can only be traversed using post-order recursion.
questions.explanation: AVL trees maintain strict height balance (|hL - hR| <= 1), providing faster lookups for read-heavy workloads. Red-Black trees tolerate slightly deeper branches (max height 2 log2(N+1)), requiring at most 2 or 3 rotations per mutation.

questions.question: When finding the shortest path in a graph with non-negative edge weights, what is the time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm implemented with a Binary Min-Heap?
options: O((V + E) log V)
O(V * E)
O(V log E + E^2)
questions.explanation: With a binary heap, each vertex extraction takes O(log V) for V vertices. Each edge relaxation can trigger a heap decrease-key operation in O(log V) for E edges, yielding O((V + E) log V).

questions.question: Which dynamic programming optimization reduces the time complexity of finding the Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) of an array of length N from O(N^2) to O(N log N)?
options: Matrix exponentiation on the adjacency list.
Patience sorting maintaining an array of smallest tail elements and using Binary Search (bisection).
Converting the array into a minimum heap.
Applying the Knapsack recursive memoization equation.
questions.explanation: Maintaining an array 'tails' where tails[i] stores the smallest tail of all increasing subsequences of length i+1 allows updating or appending candidates in O(log N) using binary search.

questions.question: What data structure pair provides optimal O(1) median retrieval and O(log N) insertion for an unbounded live data stream?
options: A single sorted dynamic circular array.
Two Heaps: A Max-Heap for the lower half and a Min-Heap for the upper half.
A FIFO queue and a LIFO stack.
A Bloom filter paired with a hash table.
questions.explanation: Balancing sizes between a max-heap (storing elements <= median) and a min-heap (storing elements >= median) keeps the median directly accessible at the heap roots in O(1) time.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Kahn's Algorithm (in-degree queue) for Topological Sorting on a Directed Acyclic Graph with V vertices and E edges?
options: O(V + E)
O(V * E)
O(E log V)
questions.explanation: Kahn's algorithm initializes in-degrees in O(V + E), pushes zero in-degree nodes into a queue, and processes each vertex and edge exactly once, completing in linear O(V + E) time.

questions.question: What is the amortized per-operation time complexity of Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) with both Path Compression and Union by Rank?
options: O(log N)
O(alpha(N)), where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function (practically <= 4).
O(N)
O(N log N)
questions.explanation: Path compression flattens tree depths during find operations, while union by rank keeps subtrees shallow. Together, they achieve near-constant amortized time O(alpha(N)) per operation.

questions.question: In Hash Table design, what phenomenon describes clustering in Open Addressing with Linear Probing?
options: Primary Clustering: Contiguous occupied bucket runs grow longer, increasing average collision probe sequences.
Garbage collection fragmentation in external pointer arrays.
Integer overflow during modular division.
Bucket starvation where only odd-indexed slots are populated.
questions.explanation: Linear probing checks bucket (hash + i) % m. Adjacent occupied slots merge into continuous clusters, drastically increasing probe counts for any key hashing into that cluster.

questions.question: Why does standard Quicksort exhibit an O(N^2) worst-case time complexity, and how is it mitigated in production libraries (e.g. Introsort)?
options: Memory allocation failures; mitigated by allocating extra swap buffers.

Unbalanced partition splits (e.g. picking minimum or maximum as pivot on sorted inputs); mitigated by Median-of-Three pivot selection and falling back to Heapsort when recursion depth exceeds threshold.
Cache misses on large arrays; mitigated by multi-threading.
Stack frame overflows; mitigated by converting all loops to goto statements.
questions.explanation: Skewed partitions (size 1 and N-1) yield quadratic recurrence. Introsort starts with Quicksort for speed, uses Median-of-Three pivots, and monitors call stack depth, switching to O(N log N) Heapsort if depth exceeds 2 * log(N).

questions.question: Which algorithm finds the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) of a connected, undirected weighted graph by sorting all edges and greedily uniting non-cyclic components?
options: Floyd-Warshall Algorithm
Kruskal's Algorithm
Kosaraju's Algorithm
Tarjan's Strongly Connected Components Algorithm
questions.explanation: Kruskal's algorithm sorts all edges by weight in O(E log E) time, then iterates through them, using Disjoint Set Union (DSU) to add edges that connect disconnected trees without forming cycles.
